title: The history of the flush toilet
tagline: 4,500 years from brick drains in the Indus cities to seats that wash, and the unfinished work of a safe toilet for everyone.
intro: People have used water to carry waste away for thousands of years, but a pipe that lets water out also lets foul air back in. In 1775 a watchmaker bent the pipe into an S, so that a little water always stayed in it as a seal. Potters, plumbers and engineers then built the pedestal, the cistern and the sewers around that idea. Today the work is to flush with far less water, and to bring a safe toilet to the billions of people who still do not have one.

eras.name: Water carries it away
eras.summary: Indus cities, Crete, China and Rome use poured or running water and drains. There is no water seal, and most people use pits and pots.

eras.name: The water closet
eras.summary: A cistern, a valve and then the S-bend trap turn the privy into a machine that flushes and keeps smells out.

eras.name: Sewers and porcelain
eras.summary: Cholera and the Great Stink force cities to build sewers. Potters make the one-piece ceramic pedestal, and the siphon arrives in bowls and cisterns.

eras.name: Less water, more comfort
eras.summary: Better fill valves, dual flush, legal limits on water per flush, vacuum toilets and the electronic seat.

eras.name: A toilet for everyone
eras.summary: Pour-flush pits, new laws, bio-toilets and huge building drives aim to end open defecation and work that robs people of dignity.

events.title: Toilets and brick drains in the Indus cities
events.where: Mohenjo-daro and Lothal (today Pakistan and India)
events.text: In Indus cities such as Mohenjo-daro, several courtyard houses had a washing platform and a toilet hole. The toilet was flushed by emptying a jar of water, which ran through a clay brick pipe into a shared brick drain and on to a soak pit. At Lothal, houses on the acropolis drained into a covered brick sewer.
events.why: Pour in water, let a sloping drain carry the waste away: it is the idea behind every flush toilet and sewer since.

events.title: A flushed seat in the palace of Knossos
events.text: A ground-floor room in the palace of Knossos has been identified as a toilet with a wooden seat. Water was poured through a hole in the floor just outside the door. A channel under the floor carried it to a clay pipe below the seat and flushed it out.
events.why: It is one of the oldest known toilets flushed with water, and it worked just like today's pour-flush pans.

events.title: Rome's great drain
events.who: Roman builders (tradition credits King Tarquinius Priscus)
events.text: The Cloaca Maxima began as open channels that drained the marshy ground around the Forum. Over time it was built over and became a covered sewer that emptied into the River Tiber. Parts of it still carry rainwater today.
events.why: It showed that a city needs big shared drains, not just private pits.

events.title: A palace toilet with a drain pipe
events.who: Builders of the Qin palace at Yueyang
events.text: Archaeologists digging in palace ruins at Yueyang found the broken parts of a toilet bowl and a bent pipe. The toilet sat on a platform indoors, and the pipe below led the waste outside. They announced the find in February 2023 and dated it to about 2,400 years ago.
events.why: Flushing with water was thought of in many places, long before anyone could buy a toilet.

events.title: Roman public latrines
events.text: Roman public latrines had long bench seats with keyhole-shaped openings, set in rows. They did not flush in the modern sense. A stream of water ran all the time in a channel underneath and carried the waste away.
events.why: Running water did the cleaning, but there was no water seal to hold back the smell of the sewer.

events.title: The castle garderobe
events.text: Medieval castles had garderobes: small rooms with a seat over a simple hole. The waste dropped down a shaft to a cesspit or into the moat. Examples survive at Peveril Castle in Derbyshire and at Chirk Castle in Wales.
events.why: It kept waste out of the living rooms but used no water at all, so nothing was washed away.

events.title: Harington's water closet
events.text: Harington, a godson of Queen Elizabeth I, built a flushing closet at his house at Kelston and described it in a book in 1596. A cistern above the seat held water, and a valve let it rush down to wash the bowl. He called it the Ajax, a play on ‘jakes’, an old word for a privy. One is said to have been put in at Richmond Palace for the Queen.
events.why: It had a cistern, a flush valve and a wash-down bowl, but no trap, so smells could still come back up the pipe.

events.title: The S-bend
events.text: Cumming, a Scottish watchmaker working in London, was granted patent number 1105 for a flushing water closet. Below the bowl, the waste pipe curved into an S shape. Water stayed in the bend after every flush and blocked foul air from the drain.
events.why: That little pool of water, the water seal, is still what keeps sewer gas out of every bathroom.

events.title: Bramah's valve closet
events.text: Bramah, who fitted water closets for a living, found faults in the designs he installed. His patent, number 1177, used a hinged flap to seal the bottom of the bowl and a handle that worked two valves at once. His closets were made well into the 1800s. He later invented the hydraulic press.
events.why: It is often called the first practical flush toilet, though it was used mainly on boats.

events.title: Spending a penny at the Great Exhibition
events.where: The Crystal Palace, Hyde Park, London, England
events.text: Jennings, a sanitary engineer, fitted flushing closets in the Retiring Rooms of the Great Exhibition. During the exhibition 827,280 visitors paid one penny to use them. For the penny they got a clean seat, a towel, a comb and a shoe shine. He patented his improved closet on 23 August 1852.
events.why: It showed that people would gladly pay for a clean public toilet, and public toilets became part of city life.

events.title: The Broad Street pump
events.text: Cholera broke out around Broad Street, and 127 people nearby died in three days. The doctor John Snow traced the cases to one street pump. He spoke to the parish on 7 September and the pump handle was taken off the next day. A leaking cesspit was later found about three feet from the well.
events.why: It showed that sewage in drinking water spreads disease, so toilets must send waste somewhere safe.

events.title: The Great Stink and London's sewers
events.text: More and more flush toilets emptied into old sewers that ran into the River Thames, and in the hot summer of 1858 the river stank so badly that Parliament acted. A law was passed on 2 August. From 1859 Bazalgette built 82 miles of main brick sewers, fed by about 1,100 miles of street sewers, to carry the waste away from the city.
events.why: A flush toilet is only as good as the sewer it is joined to.

events.title: The siphon in the bowl
events.who: John Randall Mann, William Smith and William Howell
events.text: In 1870 John Randall Mann was granted a patent for a siphonic closet fed by three pipes. William Smith patented a jet siphon closet in 1876, and in 1890 William Howell's design did away with the lower trap. In these bowls the outlet pipe fills with water and the siphon sucks the bowl empty.
events.why: The siphonic bowl became the usual design in North America, while most of the world uses the wash-down bowl.

events.title: A plumber, not the inventor
events.text: Crapper ran a London plumbing company and what is described as the world's first showroom for baths, toilets and sinks. He held nine patents, three of them for water closet improvements such as the floating ballcock, but none for the flush toilet itself. He supplied royal houses and won royal warrants.
events.why: He made the flush toilet popular; he did not invent it, as the story often says.

events.title: One piece of pottery
events.text: Earlier closets were usually boxed in a wooden cabinet. Twyford's Unitas was a free-standing pedestal made entirely of fired clay, with the pan and the trap in one piece. It was sold around the world, and ‘unitaz’ is still the Russian word for a toilet.
events.why: The bare ceramic pedestal, easy to clean all round, is the shape toilets still have.

events.title: The wash-down pedestal
events.who: The Jennings company and Frederick Humpherson
events.text: At the 1884 International Health Exhibition, the Jennings Pedestal Vase won a gold medal. In a test, a flush of 2 gallons cleared ten apples, a flat sponge and four pieces of paper. In 1885 Frederick Humpherson of the Beaufort Works in Chelsea showed the modern pedestal wash-down toilet.
events.why: In a wash-down bowl the water simply pushes the waste through the trap, the design used in India, Europe and most of the world.

events.title: A cistern with no valve to leak
events.text: Giblin received British patent 4,990 for the ‘Silent Valveless Water Waste Preventer’. Pulling the lever lifts a disc that throws water over the top of a bent tube, and the siphon then empties the cistern. There is no sealing washer to wear out. Britain required siphon cisterns until 1 January 2001, when valve flushes were allowed.
events.why: A siphon cannot drip the way a worn valve does, and it is the reason older British toilets flush with a lever and a siphon.

events.title: The flush with no tank
events.text: Sloan's Royal Flushometer was a valve that let a measured amount of water straight from the supply pipe into the bowl, with no cistern at all. He sold one in 1906 and two in 1907, then 150 by 1908.
events.why: With no tank to refill, it can be flushed again straight away, which suits busy public toilets.

events.title: A float that rides the fill valve
events.text: The ballcock, a floating ball on an arm that shuts the water off as the tank fills, was described in 1790 by the Mexican priest and scientist José Antonio de Alzate y Ramírez. In 1957 Schoepe founded Fluidmaster and brought out a fill valve with a float cup that slides up the valve tower itself.
events.why: The float cup takes less room than a ball on an arm, and it is now a common sight inside toilet tanks.

events.title: Sulabh and the twin-pit toilet
events.text: Pathak founded Sulabh to replace dry latrines that had to be emptied by hand. Its toilet has a steep squat pan and a shallow water seal, and is flushed by pouring in 1.5 to 2 litres of water. The waste runs to one of two pits. When the first pit is full the flow is switched to the second, and after about two years of rest the first holds dry, safe manure.
events.why: It needs no sewer and very little water, and Sulabh says it has built more than 1.69 million household toilets.

events.title: The vacuum toilet for aircraft
events.text: Kemper's patent, granted to Monogram Industries, used the difference between cabin pressure and a low-pressure waste tank to suck the bowl empty. Time magazine reports that the Kemper vacuum system first flew in a Boeing aircraft in 1982. A vacuum toilet can use less than a quarter of a litre of water per flush.
events.why: Suction does the work of gravity and water, which saves a great deal of weight in the air.

events.title: The Washlet
events.text: In the 1960s TOTO imported American ‘wash air seats’ for hospitals and nursing homes, and began making them in Japan in 1969. In June 1980 it launched the Washlet, an electric seat that washes the user with warm water. TOTO says it had sold 70 million by 2025.
events.why: It turned the toilet seat into an electronic appliance.

events.title: Two buttons, two flushes
events.text: TOTO had tried a dual-flush system in Japan in 1960, but it did not sell. In 1980 staff at the Australian company Caroma designed the first practical one: a full flush of 11 litres and a half flush of 5.5 litres. A redesign in 1994 cut this to 6 and 3 litres.
events.why: Most visits need only the small flush, so the two-button cistern spread around the world.

events.title: A legal limit on the flush
events.text: Older American toilets used about 13 litres a flush, and some as much as 6 gallons, nearly 23 litres. The Energy Policy Act of 1992 said that from 1994 common new toilets could use no more than 1.6 US gallons, about 6 litres. The WaterSense label, set up in 2006, goes further: 1.28 gallons, about 4.8 litres.
events.why: Engineers had to redesign the bowl and trapway to clear the same waste with less than half the water.

events.title: Laws against manual scavenging
events.text: Dry latrines have no water to carry waste away, so they had to be emptied by hand. This work is called manual scavenging. The Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 banned this. The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013 widened the ban to septic tanks, open drains and railway tracks. Government surveys in 2013 and 2018 identified 58,098 manual scavengers.
events.why: A water-seal toilet joined to a pit, tank or sewer is also a matter of human dignity.

events.title: Sanitation becomes a human right
events.text: In resolution 64/292 the UN General Assembly recognised the human right to water and sanitation. In 2013 it also made 19 November World Toilet Day, an idea started in 2001 by Jack Sim of Singapore and his World Toilet Organization.
events.why: A safe toilet stopped being seen as a luxury and became something every person is owed.

events.title: Bio-toilets on Indian trains
events.who: Indian Railways and the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)
events.text: Train toilets in India used to empty straight onto the track. Under an agreement signed in March 2010, Indian Railways and DRDO developed a tank of anaerobic bacteria that sits under the toilet and turns the waste into water and a little gas. The first set of coaches ran on the Bundelkhand Express from 18 January 2011. By 2020 the Railways reported more than 245,400 bio-toilets in 68,800 coaches.
events.why: It treats the waste on board, with living bacteria doing the work a sewer would do.

events.title: Reinvent the Toilet
events.text: The foundation challenged researchers to design a toilet that kills germs and recovers water, energy or nutrients. It must work with no sewer or water connection and very little electricity, and cost less than 5 US cents per user per day. Fairs followed in Seattle in 2012, Delhi in 2014 and Beijing in 2018.
events.why: The flush toilet needs piped water and a sewer, which billions of people do not have.

events.title: Swachh Bharat Mission
events.text: India had run a national rural sanitation programme since 1986, followed by new ones in 1999 and 2012. On 2 October 2014 Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the Swachh Bharat Mission. The government says more than 100 million toilets were built in rural India, and that every village had declared itself free of open defecation by 2 October 2019. WHO and UNICEF estimates put open defecation at about 7% of people in India in 2024.
events.why: India had more people practising open defecation than any other country, so its progress changed the numbers for the whole world.

events.title: Still 3.4 billion to go
events.text: The WHO and UNICEF reported that 3.4 billion people still lack safely managed sanitation, and 354 million of them practise open defecation. The share of the world's people practising open defecation fell from about 21% in 2000 to about 4% in 2024.
events.why: The toilet is 4,500 years old, and the job of bringing a safe one to everyone is not finished.

people.name: John Harington
people.note: Godson of Elizabeth I who built and described a flushing closet in 1596.

people.name: Alexander Cumming
people.note: Patented the S-bend trap that keeps a seal of water in the pipe.

people.name: Joseph Bramah
people.note: Patented a valve closet with a hinged flap in 1778, and later the hydraulic press.

people.name: George Jennings
people.note: Put flush toilets in the Great Exhibition of 1851 and championed public toilets.

people.name: Joseph Bazalgette
people.note: Built London's main sewers after the Great Stink of 1858.

people.name: John Snow
people.note: Traced the 1854 Soho cholera outbreak to a pump whose well was fouled by a cesspit.

people.name: Thomas William Twyford
people.note: Made the Unitas, a free-standing closet formed entirely from ceramic.

people.name: Thomas Crapper
people.note: Sold and promoted flush toilets and held nine plumbing patents, but did not invent the toilet.

people.name: Adolf Schoepe
people.note: Founded Fluidmaster in 1957 and made the float-cup fill valve common.

people.name: Bindeshwar Pathak
people.note: Founded Sulabh in 1970 and spread the twin-pit pour-flush toilet. Awarded the Padma Bhushan, the Stockholm Water Prize and, after his death, the Padma Vibhushan.

people.name: Usha Chaumar
people.note: Once a manual scavenger in Rajasthan, she became president of Sulabh's social service organisation and received the Padma Shri in 2020.

people.name: Bezwada Wilson
people.note: A founder of the Safai Karmachari Andolan (1994), which campaigns to end manual scavenging. Won the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2016.

facts: At the Great Exhibition of 1851, 827,280 visitors paid one penny each to use George Jennings's flush toilets. In Britain people still say they are going to ‘spend a penny’.
Thomas Crapper did not invent the flush toilet. He held nine plumbing patents, but none for the toilet itself.
Twyford's 1880s Unitas closet was sold so widely that ‘unitaz’ became the Russian word for a toilet.
A pour-flush squat pan with a twin pit needs only 1.5 to 2 litres of water a flush, says Sulabh, against 10 to 12 litres for an old cistern.
Toilets use nearly 30% of the water used indoors in an average American home, says the US Environmental Protection Agency.
William Sloan sold just one Flushometer in 1906 and two in 1907. Sales then took off, with 150 sold by 1908.
